lessons.title: The Instruments Used in Indian Rounds: Equity Shares, CCPS, CCDs and iSAFEs

children.text: A founder announces she raised ₹6 crore for 20%. What she actually signed was a subscription agreement for compulsorily convertible preference shares with a 1x liquidation preference, broad-based weighted average anti-dilution and a conversion ratio that adjusts on a down round. Same money, same headline percentage, very different rights. In India the instrument is not a technicality, it is where a large part of the deal lives. This lesson explains the four you will meet, and what each one costs you.

body.text: Indian investors almost never buy plain equity shares. They buy an instrument that converts into equity later, on terms agreed today. Understanding what triggers conversion, and at what price, matters more than the percentage on the headline.

children.text: The Four Instruments You Will Meet

cells: Equity shares
Plain ownership with voting and a residual claim
Founders, employees exercising ESOPs, some friends and family rounds
Simplicity, and it is what everything else eventually becomes
CCPS
Compulsorily convertible preference shares: preference shares that must convert into equity
The standard for priced seed and Series A rounds in India
Liquidation preference, anti-dilution protection and preferential rights, while still counting as equity for FDI
CCDs
Compulsorily convertible debentures: debt on the books until they convert
Occasionally in seed and growth rounds, and in structured deals
Debt-like features such as interest before conversion, with an agreed conversion into equity
Convertible notes and iSAFEs
An agreement to convert into shares at a future priced round
Pre-seed, seed and bridge rounds
Speed: the round closes without agreeing a valuation today

children.text: CCPS: The Default for Priced Rounds

markDefs.definition: Preference shares that must convert into equity shares by an agreed date or event. They cannot be redeemed for cash instead, which is what makes them count as equity under India's foreign investment rules.
The right to be paid before equity shareholders when the company is sold or wound up, usually at least the amount originally invested.

children.text: If you raise a priced round from an Indian fund, expect
CCPS
. They sit between debt and equity: the investor gets a
liquidation preference

and negotiated rights, and the shares convert into ordinary equity at an agreed ratio, usually 1:1, when the company lists or when the parties agree. Because conversion is compulsory, foreign investors can use them without falling foul of India's rules on debt-like instruments.

stats.label: Conversion
stats.context: Usually 1:1 into equity, adjustable on a down round

stats.label: Downside protection
stats.context: Investor money comes back before founders see anything

stats.label: Price protection
stats.context: Conversion ratio improves for the investor if a later round is cheaper

stats.label: Control
stats.context: A list of decisions needing investor consent, covered in Lesson 4.2

body.text: This is why "we sold 20%" tells you very little in India. Two companies can both sell 20% via CCPS, and if one carries a 1x non-participating preference and the other a 2x participating preference, the founders walk away with dramatically different amounts in a ₹100 crore exit. The percentage sets who votes. The preference decides who gets paid.

children.text: CCDs: When the Money Comes In as Debt

Compulsorily convertible debentures sit on the balance sheet as borrowings until they convert, and may carry interest in the meantime. Founders see them in structured or later rounds, and sometimes when an investor wants a return even if conversion is delayed. Like CCPS, they must convert, which is what keeps them inside the equity bucket for foreign investment purposes. The practical difference for you is accounting and interest: a CCD can create a real cash obligation before it ever becomes equity.
Convertible Notes and iSAFEs: Postponing the Valuation Argument

At pre-seed nobody can price the company honestly, so the round is often done on an instrument that says: take the money now, work out the price at the next real round. Two economic terms decide what that costs you.

markDefs.definition: A ceiling on the valuation used to convert an early investor's money into shares, however high the next round is priced.

children.text: Valuation cap:
the maximum valuation at which the early money converts. It rewards the investor for coming in first.
Discount:
a reduction on the next round's price per share, commonly 10% to 25%. When both a cap and a discount exist, the investor converts at whichever gives them more shares.

body.caption: The investor converts at the lower price, because a lower price buys more shares

children.text: Worked example. An angel puts ₹50 lakh into an illustrative Kochi startup on a note with an ₹8 crore valuation cap and a 20% discount. The company has 10,00,000 shares. Eighteen months later it raises a seed round at ₹20 crore pre-money, so the round price is ₹20 crore ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹200 per share.

body.caption: The same ₹50 lakh, converted three ways
headers: Effective stake before the new money

cells: No cap, no discount
20% discount only
₹8 crore cap
Cap and discount, investor takes the better

body.text: The cap did most of the work here, turning a 2.44% stake into 5.88%. That is the deal the founder signed 18 months earlier, probably without modelling it. A cap is a valuation, just one agreed before you know what the company will be worth. Never sign a note calling the cap "just a formality", and always model conversion at two or three plausible next-round prices before agreeing.

body.title: How many shares does the note buy?
body.prompt: An investor holds a ₹40 lakh convertible note with a ₹10 crore valuation cap. The company has 8,00,000 shares outstanding and raises its next round at ₹30 crore pre-money. Converting at the cap, how many shares does the investor receive?
body.explanation: Cap price per share is ₹10 crore ÷ 8,00,000 = ₹125. The note buys ₹40,00,000 ÷ ₹125 = 32,000 shares. Had it converted at the round price of ₹30 crore ÷ 8,00,000 = ₹375, the same money would have bought only 10,667 shares. The cap tripled the investor's position, and the founders paid for it in dilution.

body.title: Why India uses iSAFEs instead of American SAFEs

children.text: In the United States a SAFE is a contract that sits outside company law until it converts. Indian company law does not recognise that halfway state comfortably, so Indian versions are usually structured as an actual security, most commonly CCPS with the conversion economics written in. The iSAFE, introduced by the accelerator 100X.VC, is the best known Indian adaptation.

There is also a separate, specific route: the convertible note recognised under India's foreign exchange rules. It is available only to DPIIT-recognised startups, has a minimum investment size per tranche, and must convert within a prescribed period. Because those conditions are narrow and have been amended over the years, confirm the current requirements with your company secretary rather than assuming a template from a blog post applies to your company.
The practical upshot for a founder: whatever the document is called, ask three questions. What event forces conversion, at what price, and what happens if no round ever comes?

columns.label: Priced round with CCPS
points: Valuation agreed today, so dilution is known today
Full documentation, diligence and a valuation report
Slower and more expensive to close
Investor gets preference, anti-dilution and consent rights immediately
Cap table is clean and readable

columns.label: Convertible note or iSAFE
points: Valuation postponed to the next round
Cheaper legally, and easy to add investors one at a time
Dilution is unknown until conversion, and can surprise you
Several notes with different caps make the cap table hard to read

body.label: The stacking problem
body.value: Notes convert together, all at once
body.context: Raise ₹40 lakh on a ₹6 crore cap, then ₹60 lakh on a ₹9 crore cap, then ₹1 crore on a ₹14 crore cap, and all three convert at the seed round. Founders regularly discover they have given away far more than they thought, because each note was signed in isolation and nobody modelled them together.

body.title: Which instrument fits?
body.question: A DPIIT-recognised Jaipur startup with a prototype and no revenue needs ₹60 lakh quickly from two angels, and does not want to argue about valuation yet. Which instrument fits best?
options: Equity shares issued at a negotiated price per share
A convertible instrument such as an iSAFE, with a valuation cap and a discount
A bank term loan against the founders' personal guarantees
body.explanation: A convertible instrument closes fast, needs less paperwork and postpones the valuation argument until a real round prices the company. Pricing equity at prototype stage is guesswork, interest-bearing CCDs create a cash obligation the company cannot service, and a personally guaranteed loan puts the founders' own assets behind an unproven product.

body.title: The surprise at conversion
body.scenario: Over two years, Sameer raised three convertible notes for his Pune hardware startup: ₹40 lakh at a ₹6 crore cap, ₹60 lakh at a ₹9 crore cap, and ₹1 crore at a ₹14 crore cap, each with a 20% discount. The company has 10,00,000 shares held by the two founders. A seed fund now offers ₹8 crore at ₹32 crore pre-money, and expects all notes to convert as part of the round.
body.prompt: Roughly what happens to the founders' ownership, and what should Sameer have done differently?
body.modelAnswer:
Work out each conversion price against the 10,00,000 existing shares. The round price is ₹32 crore ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹320 per share, and the 20% discount gives ₹256, so every note converts at its cap because each cap price is far lower.
Note 1: cap price ₹6 crore ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹60. ₹40,00,000 ÷ ₹60 = about 66,667 shares.
Note 2: cap price ₹90. ₹60,00,000 ÷ ₹90 = about 66,667 shares.
Note 3: cap price ₹140. ₹1,00,00,000 ÷ ₹140 = about 71,429 shares.
That is roughly 2,04,763 new shares from ₹2 crore of notes, taking the pre-round count to about 12,04,763 before the seed fund's money and before any ESOP pool. The note holders end up with about 17% of the pre-round company, and the founders drop from 100% to about 83% before the seed round even starts. Add the fund's stake and a pool, and the founders are well below 65%.
What he should have done: model every note against two or three plausible next-round valuations before signing it, keep the caps consistent and rising with progress, cap the total amount raised on notes, and once the third note was needed, do a small priced round instead so the dilution was visible in advance. Notes are convenient precisely because the cost is invisible on the day you sign.

body.title: The number that matters on a note
body.textWithBlank: On a convertible note, the valuation ___ sets the highest valuation at which the early money can convert, which is why it behaves like a valuation agreed in advance.
body.explanation: However high the next round is priced, the note converts at no more than the cap. That is why a founder should model conversion at several possible round prices before agreeing a cap.

body.title: Questions to ask about any instrument you are offered
steps: What exactly is it: equity shares, CCPS, CCDs, a convertible note or an iSAFE?
What event forces conversion, and at what ratio or price?
Is there a valuation cap, a discount, or both, and which applies if they conflict?
What is the liquidation preference, and is it participating or non-participating?
Does anti-dilution protection apply, and on what basis?
If it is a CCD, is interest payable in cash before conversion?
What happens if no priced round ever occurs: does it convert anyway, and at what price?
Model the cap table after conversion, including every earlier note, before you sign.

cards.definition: Compulsorily convertible preference shares: the standard instrument in Indian priced rounds, carrying preference and protective rights before converting to equity.
Compulsorily convertible debenture: sits as debt on the books, may carry interest, and must convert into equity.
An Indian adaptation of the SAFE, usually issued as CCPS, converting at a future priced round.
The maximum valuation at which early money converts, regardless of how high the next round is priced.
A reduction on the next round's share price for early investors, commonly 10% to 25%.
The right to be paid before equity shareholders on a sale or winding up, usually at least the amount invested.
Several convertible instruments with different caps all converting at the same round, often producing more dilution than founders expected.

points: Indian investors rarely buy plain equity. Priced rounds use CCPS, and early rounds often use convertible notes or iSAFEs.
CCPS carry a liquidation preference, anti-dilution and consent rights, and count as equity under India's foreign investment rules because conversion is compulsory.
CCDs are debt until they convert and can carry interest, creating a cash obligation before any equity exists.
Convertible instruments postpone the valuation argument but not the dilution. The cap is a valuation agreed before you know what the company is worth.
When a note has both a cap and a discount, the investor converts at whichever price gives more shares. In the worked example the cap turned 2.44% into 5.88%.
Notes stack. Three notes signed in isolation converted into roughly 17% of the pre-round company in the Pune example.
Model every conversion against two or three plausible next-round prices before signing anything.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Instrument features, foreign exchange conditions for convertible notes and company law requirements change, and templates differ between investors. Verify current requirements with a qualified company secretary or lawyer before issuing any instrument. All companies, caps and figures here are illustrative and simplified.
